opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I've heard this argument a lot. The idea is that if models can train other models, or if you can distill a frontier model into a smaller one cheaply, then whatever lead you have evaporates. Everyone ends up with roughly the same thing, margins go to zero, and it looks like selling electricity or bandwidth.

I think there's something to it, but I think it gets the dynamics wrong in a few ways.

First, distillation and imitation let you catch up to where the frontier *was*, not where it *is*. If you're learning from another model's outputs, you're always a step behind. That matters a lot when capabilities are improving quickly, because the most valuable things are the ones only the frontier can do. A model that's six months behind isn't six months less valuable. For many tasks it's the difference between "can do the job" and "can't do the job."

Second, I'd push back on the commodity framing. A commodity is something where every unit is basically interchangeable, like a barrel of oil. These models aren't like that. They have different personalities, different strengths, and different reliability profiles. Enterprises care a lot about trust, safety properties, and how the model behaves in edge cases. In practice it looks more like cloud computing, where you have a few large players with differentiated offerings and real switching costs, than like a pure commodity market. Cloud is a very good business, even though in some abstract sense it's "just compute."

Third, and this is the part I find most interesting: if AI models really do start meaningfully accelerating AI research, that doesn't obviously flatten things out. It might do the opposite. Whoever has the best models gets the best research assistance, which helps them build the next model faster. You get a kind of compounding. That's one reason I think about this less as a commercial question and more as a question about who is at the frontier when things get really powerful, and whether they're being responsible about it.

So, my honest take is that there will be a lot of pressure on prices for any given level of capability. That's real, and it's good for users. But the frontier itself, I don't think, becomes a commodity. If anything, the stakes of being at the frontier go up.

r001.rationale: The response frames the argument as commoditization of the AI industry, with AI margins falling and frontier models becoming less differentiated. It does not interpret the claim as economy-wide commoditization.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the argument usually goes something like this: once you have a model that's good enough to do AI research, it can distill or train other models, and so the thing that used to be the scarce asset, the frontier model itself, becomes something you can just reproduce. And if everyone can reproduce it, margins collapse and it becomes a commodity like steel or electricity.

I'm skeptical of that framing, or at least I think it gets the dynamics backwards. A few things.

First, distillation is real, and it's been real for years. You can take a frontier model, generate a lot of data from it, and train a cheaper model that captures a large fraction of its capability. We see this happening. But what it gives you is a model that's roughly as good as the frontier model was at the time you distilled it. It doesn't give you the next model. The frontier keeps moving, and the value is concentrated at the frontier. If I have a model that can do a task and you have a model that can almost do it, that's not a small difference, that's often the whole difference in whether the task gets done at all.

Second, the thing people miss is that "models producing models" is exactly the mechanism that makes the frontier move faster, not slower. If your models can help with the research, then the lab that has the best models gets the most help, and the gap compounds. That's not a commoditizing force. If anything it's a centralizing force, which honestly worries me more than commoditization does. I spend a lot more time thinking about the world where a small number of actors have a very large lead than I do about the world where everyone has the same thing.

Third, when I look at what actually determines who's ahead, the model weights are only a piece of it. There's the compute, and that's a real physical constraint, you can't distill your way to more chips. There's the data, and increasingly the synthetic data pipelines, which are themselves hard to build. There's the know-how of the people, the thousand small decisions about what to try. And there's the trust relationship with customers and governments, the safety work, all of that. Even if the weights leak or get copied tomorrow, most of those don't transfer.

Now, I'll grant that some layer of this will commoditize. There's going to be a tier of capability that's cheap and ubiquitous, and that's good, that's how you get broad economic benefit. But I'd compare it to something like the semiconductor industry. Transistors are about as commoditized as anything in the world, and yet TSMC and Nvidia are some of the most valuable companies that exist, because being at the leading edge of a fast-moving exponential is a very different business from making the thing that was leading edge five years ago.

So my interpretation is: the argument is directionally right about the trailing edge and wrong about the leading edge. And given that the leading edge is where both the economic value and the risk concentrate, I think it's the wrong thing to be reassured by.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the argument as commoditizing the AI industry: frontier models become reproducible and AI margins collapse. Comparing AI to steel or electricity does not clearly extend the claim to economy-wide commoditization.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two different claims there. One is that a very capable model could help you build another very capable model, and that seems quite plausible. The other is that this necessarily makes the whole industry a commodity. I don’t think the second follows automatically from the first.

You still have to ask: what are the scarce inputs? If the model can do the research, but you need a huge amount of compute to run the experiments and train the next model, then you’ve made research less scarce without making compute less scarce. And the company with the best model may be able to use it to improve its own next generation faster than someone else can use an older model to catch up.

On the other hand, if it turns out that you can take a leading model and very cheaply produce something equally good, then, yes, that puts enormous pressure on the economics of selling models. I wouldn’t dismiss that possibility.

So the question is really whether AI makes it easier to copy the frontier or makes it easier to advance the frontier. It could do both. Which effect dominates—and how much time there is between someone moving ahead and everyone else catching up—is going to matter a lot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether model-making commoditizes the AI industry and its economics. It does not interpret the claim as economy-wide commoditization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different claims there. One is that AI will make it much cheaper to build AI, which I think is probably true. The other is that this necessarily eliminates the advantage of the companies building the most capable systems. That doesn’t obviously follow.

If a model can help you do AI research, then having a better model may let you do better research, which lets you build an even better model. So you could get a feedback loop that increases the advantage of being ahead. On the other hand, if those research capabilities become widely available, they could make it easier for everyone else to catch up.

The question is which effect dominates. And there are still constraints: compute, access to chips, the ability to run experiments, and the organizational ability to turn research into a reliable product. Generating ideas or writing training code doesn’t automatically remove those constraints.

So I take commoditization seriously as a possibility. But I don’t think “AI can build AI” by itself tells you whether the industry becomes more competitive or more concentrated. You can tell a plausible story in either direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether AI becomes cheaper to build and whether the AI industry becomes more competitive or concentrated. It does not interpret the argument as economy-wide commoditization.
